families.name: The finite expansion and the mean

meaning: Each tie is a pointer that landed. Whether the paper and the Lean say the same thing is a reading.

rows.fidelity_note: The paper’s sentence asserts finite-time blow-up from smooth periodic initial data. The formal theorem additionally chooses odd divergence-free data, proves bounded velocity and central vorticity divergence, gives both divergent time integrals, and supplies every off-origin spatial limit. These are stronger conclusions for the same selected solution; they do not apply to every smooth initial datum.
rows.name: TorusEuler.theorem11

rows.fidelity_note: For the chosen smooth periodic solution on $[0,T_*)$, the selected clause requires one finite real constant $C$ with $\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}\le C$ for every $0\le t<T_*$. This is the abstract’s uniform velocity bound. The clause describes the solution required by the theorem; existence is supplied by Theorem 1.1.
rows.name: TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness

rows.fidelity_note: For the selected solution with $T_*>0$, the formal clause is the full limit $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$ as $t\uparrow T_*$ through $[0,T_*)$. It is not merely unboundedness along a subsequence. The pointwise vector norm is Euclidean.
rows.name: TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness

rows.fidelity_note: The selected clauses require the velocity and its time derivative to have uniform limits of all spatial derivatives on every compact set away from the integer lattice, which represents the punctured torus. This is the abstract’s spatial-limit assertion for the chosen periodic solution. It does not assert joint smoothness through the terminal time.
rows.name: TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness

rows.fidelity_note: The paper asserts the property for both $u$ and $\partial_tu$ of the constructed Euler solution. This separate definition concerns a single arbitrary field $f$: for each compact set and order $m$, its derivatives through $m$ must converge uniformly to one local $C^m$ field. It does not assert that either Euler field satisfies the condition, and imposes neither periodicity nor $T>0$ on its own.
rows.name: TorusEuler.HasOffOriginLimits
rows.plain: Spatial limits away from the origin

rows.fidelity_note: The paper’s sentence asserts finite-time blow-up from smooth periodic initial data. The formal theorem additionally chooses odd divergence-free data, proves bounded velocity and central vorticity divergence, gives both divergent time integrals, and supplies every off-origin spatial limit. These are stronger conclusions for the same selected solution; they do not apply to every smooth initial datum.
rows.name: TorusEuler.theorem11

rows.fidelity_note: The formal domain is the closed cube $[-1/2,1/2]^3\subset\mathbb R^3$, with Lebesgue measure. It is the same fundamental cell used in the paper. Opposite faces are identified by requiring the fields to be invariant under integer translations; the set defining the cube does not itself impose this condition. Including both faces does not change integrals or essential suprema, since the boundary has zero volume.
rows.name: TorusEuler.centeredCell

rows.fidelity_note: The paper identifies opposite faces of the unit cube. The formal statement uses fields on $\mathbb R^3$ invariant under every integer translation, which gives the same unit-torus representation. Periodicity imposes no regularity by itself.
rows.name: TorusEuler.SpatiallyPeriodic

rows.fidelity_note: The selected clauses are exactly $\partial_tu+D_xu\,u+\nabla p=0$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on $0\le t<T_*$. In the surrounding formal definition $u,p$ are smooth periodic fields with mean-zero pressure and $T_*>0$. Time differentiation is from within the interval, hence from the right at zero; these are the classical solution conventions used in the paper.
rows.name: TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem constructs smooth odd divergence-free data with bounded velocity and central vorticity divergence, and also gives every spatial derivative limit on compact sets away from the origin. These precise conclusions support the paper’s description of concentrated growth; they do not assert that vorticity is supported only at the origin. The theorem additionally gives maximality and both divergent time integrals.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_1_1

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement retains the smooth odd periodic data, the positive finite maximal lifespan, both divergent time integrals, bounded velocity, central vorticity divergence and both families of spatial $C^m$ limits. It spells out that every maximal solution from the chosen datum has the same lifespan and velocity. This makes the paper’s classical uniqueness explicit; it does not add an Euler extension after the singularity.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_1_1

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem proves the full stated existence assertion, with all conclusions referring to one chosen datum, solution and endpoint. Periodic fields on $\mathbb R^3$ represent the unit torus, time derivatives at zero are from the right, and pressure has zero mean as stipulated in the paper’s conventions.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_1_1

rows.fidelity_note: The paper refers to the maximal classical solution of its selected datum. The formal definition specifies what maximal means: a smooth periodic solution on $[0,T_*)$ has no smooth extension to any longer interval agreeing in velocity. It neither asserts existence nor proves uniqueness. Those assertions occur in the complete theorem.
rows.name: TorusEuler.IsMaximalEulerSolution

rows.fidelity_note: Given two smooth periodic Euler solutions with the same initial velocity, the formal theorem proves equality on $[0,\min(T_1,T_2))$. This proves the velocity-uniqueness ingredient in the paper’s phrase. It assumes both solutions exist, does not assume maximality, and does not by itself identify their lifespans.
rows.name: TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution.velocity_eq_on_common_interval

rows.fidelity_note: The formal condition requires the chosen Euler velocity to be jointly smooth on $[0,T_*)\times\mathbb R^3$ and periodic there, and separately requires $u(t,-x)=-u(t,x)$ for every $0\le t<T_*$. These clauses express both smoothness and oddness in the quoted phrase; the smooth-Euler condition alone does not include oddness.
rows.name: TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness

rows.fidelity_note: The formal solution condition takes $T_*$ to be a real number and explicitly assumes $0<T_*$. Hence it is a positive finite time, not an extended-real endpoint. This is a requirement on the selected solution; it is the theorem, not this clause, that supplies such a solution.
rows.name: TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution

rows.fidelity_note: The paper asserts both limits for its Euler solution. This linked definition only specifies convergence for one given field: for every compact set and $m$, there is a local $C^m$ limit whose spatial derivatives through $m$ are the uniform limits. It does not assert the condition for $u$ or $\partial_tu$ and does not itself impose periodicity or a positive endpoint.
rows.name: TorusEuler.HasOffOriginLimits
rows.plain: Spatial limits away from the origin

rows.fidelity_note: Both statements assert that a solution satisfying all of Theorem 1.1 can be chosen with a smooth space-time extension through $T_*$ away from the torus origin. The formal statement also makes the maximal-solution uniqueness explicit. It requires no Euler equation after $T_*$, and does not quantify over every singular Euler solution.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.remark_1_2

rows.fidelity_note: The formal theorem proves the existential extension assertion for a solution with all of Theorem 1.1’s properties. Its extension need not solve Euler after $T_*$. This matches the remark; the stronger extension for all real times used in the auxiliary construction is a sufficient input, not an additional claim of the quoted sentence.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.remark_1_2

rows.fidelity_note: The paper directs the reader to the auxiliary note for the extension in Remark 1.2. The formal proof instead invokes an auxiliary existence theorem that chooses one exponent and threshold, then a solution with a smooth extension. This suffices for the existential remark. It does not prove the broader auxiliary statement for every threshold satisfying the note’s additional bounds.
rows.name: TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.remark_1_2

rows.fidelity_note: The introduction asserts existence of smooth approximate solutions with vanishing residuals. The formal theorem chooses one admissible frequency schedule and constructs smooth odd periodic divergence-free velocities with the uniform bound $|R_j|\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$, together with support, increment and crossing estimates. The frequency schedule diverges, so the residual bound implies the quoted convergence. The theorem provides additional properties for the same sequence.
rows.name: TorusEuler.paperTheorem71

rows.fidelity_note: The paper asserts existence of the sequence. The formal condition lists properties required of a given construction, including smoothness and the residual bound $|R_j|\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$ on its stage interval. It does not construct a sequence or, by itself, prove that the frequencies diverge. The separate existence theorem supplies a construction satisfying it.
rows.name: TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions

rows.fidelity_note: The paper asserts that the constructed sequence converges in spatial $C^m$ uniformly before $T_*$. This linked condition requires the stronger spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ convergence for given fields, also requires uniform velocity convergence through the accumulation time, and records agreement with any maximal solution. It does not assert existence of fields satisfying those requirements. Its accumulation time is not yet asserted to equal the maximal lifespan.
rows.name: TorusEuler.PaperLimitAgreement

rows.fidelity_note: The visible statement assumes an inductive sequence, $\lambda_0\ge2$, activation times tending to $T>0$, and every stage defined through $T$. It supplies a smooth periodic Euler limit with spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ convergence uniformly on $[0,S]$ for every $S<T$ and every nonnegative integer $m$, and uniform velocity convergence through $T$. This is stronger convergence than the quoted $C^m$ assertion, but the sequence is assumed and equality of $T$ with the maximal lifespan is established later. The assumed sequence carries the frequency and order schedule of Theorem 7.1, activation times with $0\le t_{j+1}-t_j\le\tau_j$, and smooth odd divergence-free periodic $U_j$ on $[0,S_j]$ with $\|U_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_j$, Fourier support in $|k|\le2\lambda_j^5$, $\|R_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$, $\|O_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_j^{-1}$, $\|U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$ for $m\le q_j$, $O_j=0$ before $t_j$ for $j\ge2$, and $O_j$ supported within $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ of the integer lattice. The spatial norm is the sum of supremum and one-half Hölder seminorms through order $m$.
rows.name: TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStages.paper_proposition_8_1
rows.plain: Stages converge to an Euler flow

rows.fidelity_note: The selected clauses require the oscillation at stage $j$ to be supported within distance $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ of the integer lattice and bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1}$ throughout the stage interval. This quantifies localization and small velocity, and is stronger in time than smallness only initially. The linked object is a condition on an existing construction, however; these clauses do not by themselves construct successively higher-frequency waves.
rows.name: TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions

rows.fidelity_note: For a given construction, the formal condition requires activation times $t_j$ tending to a finite positive $T$, with $T<S_j$ for every stage. Together with its monotonicity clauses, this gives a finite sum of successive activation intervals. The condition itself does not assert existence of those times and does not say that the overlapping lengths $S_j-t_j$ have this sum. This is the precise interpretation of the introductory growth intervals.
rows.name: TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions

ties.name: TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave
ties.plain: Exact waves over a linear background

rows.fidelity_note: The paper assumes smooth $D$ with zero trace and symmetric $D'+D^2$. The formal theorem retains trace and symmetry but requires only a time derivative on an interval with unique relative derivatives. It proves the Euler identity under this weaker background regularity; the profile and wave hypotheses remain necessary.
rows.name: TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave
rows.plain: Exact waves over a linear background

rows.fidelity_note: The paper defines the perturbation $w=\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$ and requires $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$. The formal formula defines the full velocity $u=Dx+w$ on $\mathbb R^3$ and imposes no transversality. Subtracting $Dx$ gives the displayed perturbation; perpendicularity is a separate assumption.
rows.name: TorusEuler.affineWaveVelocity

rows.fidelity_note: The paper introduces a transverse plane-wave ansatz. The formal theorem uses that ansatz as an input and proves the Euler equations after also assuming the two wave equations, differentiability of $F$, $P'=F$, zero trace and symmetric $D'+D^2$. It is the theorem using the formula, rather than a definition of $w$.
rows.name: TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave
rows.plain: Exact waves over a linear background

ties.name: TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave
ties.plain: Exact waves over a linear background

rows.fidelity_note: For $\operatorname{tr}D=0$, symmetric $D'+D^2$, transverse wave data and the two equations (1.4), the formal theorem proves the same Euler identity with the displayed pressure. It requires only differentiable $F$ and $P'=F$, omitting the paper’s smoothness, oddness and periodicity assumptions. Time derivatives are relative to an interval with unique derivatives.
rows.name: TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave
rows.plain: Exact waves over a linear background

rows.fidelity_note: On a specified time interval $J$, the formal condition requires $k_t=-D^Tk$ and $\mathbf a_t=-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ at every time in $J$. These are exactly the displayed evolution equations with the coefficient substituted. Derivatives are taken within $J$, hence one-sided at included endpoints. The condition alone imposes neither $k\ne0$ nor $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$; those are separate wave hypotheses. Its quotient is assigned zero at $k=0$, a case excluded in the introductory wave.
rows.name: TorusEuler.PaperAffine.WaveOn

rows.fidelity_note: The paper displays two differential equations and the pressure coefficient. This formal definition supplies only $p_{\rm w}=2k\cdot D\mathbf a/|k|^2$; it does not assert either evolution equation. The quotient is assigned zero at $k=0$, whereas the introductory wave has $k\ne0$.
rows.name: TorusEuler.affineWavePressureCoeff

rows.fidelity_note: With $S=D'+D^2$, the formal formula is $-x\cdot Sx/2-p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$, the same pressure. It is a definition; the facts that $S$ is symmetric and $P'=F$ are imposed when its gradient is used.
rows.name: TorusEuler.affineWavePressure

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement proves the same cancellation for any $k,\mathbf a,x$ with $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$, assuming only that $F$ is differentiable at $k\cdot x$. The paper’s smooth odd periodic profile and time-dependent wave equations are unnecessary for this pointwise spatial identity.
rows.name: TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection

ties.name: TorusEuler.affineWave_materialAcceleration
ties.plain: Material acceleration of an affine wave

rows.fidelity_note: The paper states phase transport and cancellation of the remaining acceleration by wave pressure. The formal statement gives only the acceleration formula $(D'+D^2)x+(\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a)F$, assuming phase transport and transversality. It does not itself state the pressure cancellation or the separate phase identity.
rows.name: TorusEuler.affineWave_materialAcceleration
rows.plain: Material acceleration of an affine wave

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement proves $\nabla p=-Sx-p_{\rm w}F(k\cdot x)k$ for symmetric $S$ and $P'=F$ at the phase. The paper’s cancellation follows after taking $S=D'+D^2$ and using $\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a=p_{\rm w}k$; neither the wave equation nor phase transport is a conclusion of this spatial identity.
rows.name: TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_affineWavePressure

rows.fidelity_note: The paper asserts preservation of perpendicularity along an interval. The formal statement proves only the pointwise derivative identity $(k\cdot\mathbf a)'=0$ from the wave equations and $k\ne0$, without assuming an initial zero pairing. To obtain preservation one must apply the identity throughout an interval and use $k(t_0)\cdot\mathbf a(t_0)=0$.
rows.name: TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_affineWavePairing_zero

ties.name: TorusEuler.hasFDerivAt_planeWave
ties.plain: Spatial derivative of a plane wave

rows.fidelity_note: The paper gives the central gradient under $F'(0)=1$. The formal statement proves $\nabla w(x)=F'(k\cdot x)\mathbf a\otimes k$ at every phase where $F$ is differentiable. Substitution of $x=0$ and the normalization yields the paper’s formula; no periodicity or wave equation is needed.
rows.name: TorusEuler.hasFDerivAt_planeWave
rows.plain: Spatial derivative of a plane wave

rows.fidelity_note: The paper defines the three frame vectors and the time-dependent strength $\sigma=|k_p||\mathbf a_p|$. This formal definition gives the frame vectors only. For nonzero perpendicular data it is the same oriented orthonormal frame; normalization at a zero vector is defined as zero.
rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame

rows.fidelity_note: The paper’s $\sigma$ in this introductory display varies with time. The formal definition is the frozen value $|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$ at activation. It agrees with the display only at $t=t_0$; it is the later frozen parameter of Section 2.2.1.
rows.name: TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmplification.initialStrength

rows.fidelity_note: For nonzero preceding data and a nonzero time scale $r$, the formal identity is $S(\sigma_p(t)/\sigma_p(0))E_2\otimes E_1=r^{-1}\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p$, where $S=\sigma_p(0)/r$. Multiplying by $r$ gives the paper’s rank-one identity. It is an identity of linear maps; identifying it with the wave’s central gradient also uses $F\prime(0)=1$.

Put $M=DU\circ X$, $\kappa=DX^{-T}k_*$, $\mathbf d=DX^{-T}\nabla_a$, $A_1=g\mathbf aF_h$, and $S=\widetilde\chi'A_1$ in the centered cell. The requirements include $R=R_U\circ X$, $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$, $\mathsf p_1=\widetilde\chi\mathsf p[A_1]$, and $C_1=B_1=\bar q_1=0$. For $1\le p\le P$, $C_{p+1}=\mathbf d\times[-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V_p/|\kappa|^2)]$. For $2\le p\le P$, require $B_{p,t}+MB_p+\mathbf d\bar q_p=-\langle H_p\rangle_s-\mathbf1_{p=2}R$ and $V_{p,t}+MV_p+\kappa\mathsf p_{p,s}=-(H_p-\langle H_p\rangle_s)+f_p^S$. Here $H_p$ is the sum of the preceding linear correction and all lower-level quadratic interactions, with the activation correction subtracted at level two; $f_p^S=-\sum_{i=2}^p(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_s(V_{p+1-i}+C_{p+1-i})$. Means satisfy $B_p=DX\,z_{p,t}$, $\operatorname{div}_az_{p,t}=0$, $z_p(0)=z_p(T)=0$ and zero spatial pressure mean. Transverse velocities are perpendicular to $\kappa$, centered and initially zero, with centered pressure. Finally $V_{P+1}=B_{P+1}=0$. This condition asserts no existence or estimates.
